the callus culture of R. rosea produces 11 phenylpropa-noids, which differ from the phenylpropanoic acids of roseroot, and triandrin was found to be a new phenylpropanoid of the plant.
The phenolic content and composition of the callus culture of R. rosea is different from that of its plant material, and the callus culture can be used for the production of phenolic compounds.
the biomass of a suspension culture of roserot stonecrop contained the highest amount of triandrin, which was 1.5-fold higher than that in the biomass of the callus culture.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of phenylpropanoid biosynthesis and accumulation in callus and suspension culture of R. rosea.

the isolation and identification of phenylpropanoid glycosides and their aglycones, as well as with the determination of their contents in the biomass of a suspension culture and in the roots of roseroot.
the isolation and characterization of phenylpropanoid glycosides from the callus culture of R. rosea and the study of their biological activity.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the callus and suspension culture biomasses contain 11 phenylpropans, including 4 new ones, and that the content of triandrin in them is about 0.1%.
phenylpropanoid biosynthesis in callus cultures of R. rosea is similar to that of other plants.
the phenylpropanoid composition and the triandrin content of the roseroot callus and suspension culture are different from those of the wild-growing plants and the cultivated roseroot.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the callus culture of R. rosea can be a good alternative to the biomass of a wild plant for obtaining the phenylpropanoid components.
the callus culture of R. rosea can be used to synthesize a variety of phenylpropanoid compounds and to accumulate triandrin.
the phenylpropanoid contents of the biomass of the callus culture are significantly higher than the contents of the biomass in the suspension culture.
The main takeaway from our work is that
callus cultures of roseroot can be used to produce triandrin, a phenylpropanoid that exhibits a wide variety of biological activity.
the phenylpropanoid content in callus cultures of R. rosea is higher than in suspension cultures.
the phenylpropanoid composition of the biomass of the callus culture is different from that of the biomass of a suspension culture and is similar to that of the plant.
